target.text: No official GLA or UK Government target established for this indicator - this is a regulatory classification, not a target.

source.name: Environment Agency / Defra - Water stressed areas: 2021 classification
source.notes: Thames Water - which supplies Lewisham - was classified as an area of 'serious' water stress in both the original 2013 determination and the 2021 update; the classification has not changed between rounds, so no numeric trend applies here (this is a one-off regulatory determination, not an annual measurement). In 2021 several other companies (e.g. Severn Trent, Wessex Water, South Staffordshire) moved from 'not serious' to 'serious' for the first time, widening the list, but Thames Water's own status was unchanged. The determination is used to decide which water companies can introduce compulsory water metering for all customers.

target.text: Reduce Thames Water's average per capita water use to 110 litres/person/day by 2050, matching the Environment Act 2021 national statutory target (122 litres/person/day by March 2038 from the 2019/20 baseline).
target.source_body: Defra / Environment Act 2021 target framework; Thames Water's government-approved WRMP24 (October 2024)

threshold.description: Environment Act 2021 target: 122 l/p/d by March 2038 (from a 2019/20 baseline); 110 l/p/d by 2050, which Thames Water's approved WRMP24 commits to matching.

source.name: Environment Agency / Defra - Water resources 2025 to 2026: analysis of the water industry's annual water resources performance
source.notes: Replaces the previous England-wide snapshot with Thames Water's own company-level per capita consumption (PCC), more granular and more relevant to Ladywell (entirely within Thames Water's supply area) than the national average - the earlier session's note that company-level data 'could not be downloaded... blocked by this environment's network egress policy' did not hold on retry; both data.gov.uk and the EA's gov.uk report pages were directly fetchable. 2025/26 figure (139.01 l/p/d) taken directly from the EA's published report tables - the England-wide average for the same year is 136.87 l/p/d, slightly lower, confirming Thames Water's own PCC genuinely runs a little above the national figure (correcting an earlier version of this indicator that implied otherwise by substituting the national figure for Lewisham's actual supplier). Earlier years (2019/20-2024/25) are Thames Water's own 'Average household - pcc' figures from the same WRMP Annual Review Data workbook used for the leakage indicator below (data.gov.uk dataset 87b59684-3da3-45cf-8881-e4727cfd1415, file 'Annual Review Historic Data- For publication 17112025.xlsx', one tab per year). The 2024/25 figure from that workbook (137.69) matches the EA's separately-published 2024/25 report (137.70) almost exactly, cross-confirming both sources. The 2025/26 figure isn't yet in that workbook (published before that year's data existed), so it's taken from the EA's standalone 2025/26 report instead.

trend.note: Environment Act 2021 baseline year (national baseline is 140 l/p/d; Thames Water's own 2019/20 figure was higher, at 145)

local_ecological.indicator: River water body status (Ravensbourne, Catford to Deptford)

threshold.description: Good ecological status (Water Framework Directive scale: high, good, moderate, poor, bad)

source.name: Environment Agency - Catchment Data Explorer, Ravensbourne (Catford to Deptford) water body GB106039023270
source.notes: Classifications CSV (data updated 17 March 2025). The EA published 2025 classifications on 6 August 2026, but as of 20 November 2026 the Catchment Data Explorer still shows 2022 as the latest year for this water body. The water body's geometry was intersected with the ONS 2022 ward boundary: it runs through Ladywell (Ladywell Fields); the upstream Keston-to-Catford water body (GB106039023260) does not. Ecological status: 2009 Poor, 2010 Poor, 2011 Bad, 2012 Bad, 2013 Poor (cycle 2; cycle 1 rated 2013 Moderate), 2014 Moderate, 2015 Moderate, 2016 Moderate, 2019 Moderate, 2022 Moderate. Classification methods change between planning cycles (cycle 1 to 2009-15, cycle 3 for 2019 and 2022), so no line is drawn. In 2022: fish Bad, invertebrates Moderate, macrophytes Poor, phosphate Poor, dissolved oxygen and ammonia High. Chemical status failed in 2019 (PFOS and PBDEs); in 2022 it is listed as 'does not require assessment'. Designated heavily modified. Reasons for not achieving good status (cycle 3) include physical modification (flood protection structures, barriers to fish, urbanisation), sewage discharges, leaking sewers and misconnected household drains (confirmed for invertebrates). Objectives CSV: ecological Good by 2027 (low confidence), overall Good by 2063.

target.text: No official target for impervious surface. The London Environment Strategy aims for at least 50% of London to be green by 2050.

local_ecological.indicator: % of land not covered by vegetation (proxy for impervious surface)

source.name: Greater London Authority - Green Cover 2024 (ward and borough statistics)
source.notes: Proxy: 100% minus the GLA's 2024 green cover estimate. It counts everything not vegetated - roofs, roads, paving, bare ground and open water - so it slightly overstates sealed surfaces where there is water or bare soil. Ladywell: ward area 204.26 ha, green 95.16 ha (46.59%), so 53.4% not vegetated. Lewisham: 39.06% green, 60.9% not. London: 51.68% green, 48.3% not. Both 2024 maps were modelled by the GLA from 25cm colour and infrared aerial imagery plus height data, captured mainly in 2022 (GLA Methodology Report, Canopy & Green Cover 2024, June 2024). Typical standard error for an average-sized ward is about 0.6 percentage points for canopy and 1.2 for green cover. The GLA says the 2024 estimates should not be compared with the 2018 Curio Canopy map (2016 imagery): the new model uses height data, and the apparent London-wide fall from 21.06% to 19.56% is 'not an indication of true change' (section 4.3). No time series is therefore drawn.

target.text: No numeric target. The LNRS sets London's biodiversity priorities and maps where nature recovery could happen.

local_ecological.indicator: % of land identified for nature recovery (London Local Nature Recovery Strategy)

source.name: Greater London Authority / GiGL - London Local Nature Recovery Strategy (LNRS) open data layers (April 2026)
source.notes: Area of the union of 'Potential measure locations' polygons inside the ONS 2022 ward boundary, divided by ward area: 54.2 ha of 204.2 ha = 26.5%. Lewisham 19.5% (683.7 of 3,514.8 ha, ONS LAD BFC); Greater London 28.4% (44,618 of 157,340 ha, ONS Region December 2022 BFC, the same boundary basis as ward and borough). Priorities assigned to the Ladywell locations: parks and open spaces, woodland, floodplain, lowland meadow, rivers and streams, ponds and lakes, scrub and urban mosaic habitat. Areas of Particular Importance for Biodiversity (APIB) in the open layer cover 0% of Ladywell (3.2% of Lewisham, 6.2% of London), but the open layer includes only nationally designated sites, Local Nature Reserves and ancient woodland: Local Wildlife Sites (SINCs) are excluded for licensing reasons (GiGL metadata, 7 April 2026), so local sites in Ladywell are not counted. The 'Areas that could become of particular importance' layer covers 1.9 ha (0.9%). Potential measure locations are opportunities, not designations.

Lewisham 2024: 261.7 ktoe (3,044 GWh) for 301,255 residents = 10.1 MWh; domestic use 5.3 MWh per resident. London (E12000007) 14.0 MWh; England (E92000001) 19.2 MWh. local_ecological.indicator: % of electricity use matched by solar generated in the borough

source.name: DESNZ - Regional Renewable Statistics: renewable electricity by local authority 2014-2025 (September 2026); Total final energy consumption 2005-2024
source.notes: Solar PV generation in Lewisham (MWh) divided by Lewisham's electricity consumption from the total final energy consumption tables (ktoe x 11.63). 2024: 7,078 MWh of 641.7 GWh = 1.1%. Installed solar capacity rose from 3.3 MW (2015) to 9.9 MW (2024) and 11.0 MW (2025). Solar is the only renewable source with published Lewisham generation: the borough also has 35 MW of municipal solid waste (energy-from-waste) capacity, whose generation is suppressed ([X]) from 2019 for confidentiality, so a full renewable share cannot be calculated. 2025 is not used: DESNZ notes many 2025 installations could not yet be assigned to a local authority, and 2025 consumption is not published. London series uses the sum of London local authority rows (installations not assigned to any authority are excluded).

source.name: Defra UK-AIR - Modelled background pollution data (PCM 1x1 km annual mean maps, 2015-2024)
source.notes: Area-weighted mean of the 1x1 km background cells overlapping the ONS 2022 Ladywell ward boundary (7 cells), from mapno2YYYY.csv, mappm25YYYYg.csv and mappm10YYYYg.csv. Ladywell NO2 2015-2024: 25.4, 26.3, 25.4, 24.0, 23.5, 21.0, 22.3, 21.4, 18.3, 18.5; PM2.5: 11.0, 12.4, 12.3, 12.5, 12.0, 10.1, 8.8, 9.4, 8.3, 9.0; PM10: 17.2, 18.5, 17.8, 18.6, 18.4, 16.6, 15.2, 17.1, 14.0, 14.4. 2024 comparators (same method): Lewisham NO2 17.5, PM2.5 9.0, PM10 14.2; London (ONS region) NO2 15.9, PM2.5 8.5, PM10 13.7. Background maps represent levels away from the immediate influence of busy roads. Defra: 'The models are continually updated and improved and so the methodology often changes each year... Users should be mindful of these year to year changes when comparing model outputs between years.' Exceedance (moved from the former separate indicator; TfL/GLA LAEI 2022 Population Exposure statistics, November 2025, data.london.gov.uk/dataset/london-atmospheric-emissions-inventory-laei-2022-2lg5g): in 2022, 0 of Lewisham's 298,700 residents lived where NO2 exceeded the 40 µg/m³ legal limit; 272,900 (91.4%) lived above 20 µg/m³, the WHO's strictest interim target and the EU limit from 2030 (London 70.2%); every Londoner lived above the WHO 2021 guideline of 10. London: about 161,000 people above the NO2 legal limit in 2019, just over 1,000 in 2022. LAEI's 20m model gave a Ladywell area mean of 21.9 µg/m³ NO2 in 2022 (27.6 in 2019), including roadside cells, so it is not joined to the PCM series. WHO 2021 guidelines: NO2 10, PM2.5 5, PM10 15 (Ladywell PM10 was below 15 in 2023 and 2024). Defra published 2025 modelled maps on 9 October 2026 (Air quality compliance assessment 2025) from a new model, CMAQ-Urban; that is a method break, so 2025 is not added to this PCM line.

target.text: No official target for local air temperature.

local_ecological.indicator: Summer air temperature compared with the London average (°C)

source.name: GLA - Properties Vulnerable to Heat Impacts in London (Arup, 2024): LSOA air temperature (T2) layer
source.notes: The geodatabase's T2 field is the high-resolution air temperature at the surface produced by Arup, averaged over summer daytime 2018-2022 for each 2021 LSOA (described in the GLA London Climate Risk Maps metadata, September 2024, which uses it as its 'mean air temperature' layer: data.london.gov.uk/dataset/climate-risk-mapping-2oxg6). Area-weighted means (weighting by LSOA area gives more weight to large, green outer-London LSOAs; the unweighted London LSOA mean, 18.07°C, would give a gap of about +0.14 to +0.19°C): Ladywell's 7 LSOAs 18.21°C, Lewisham 18.05°C, London (4,994 LSOAs) 17.96°C, so Ladywell is 0.25°C warmer than London's average and Lewisham 0.09°C. LSOA values in Ladywell range from 18.00°C to 18.75°C (Lewisham 011A and 011D share an identical value, 18.754°C, so they sit in one model cell; T2 has only 1,974 distinct values across 4,994 LSOAs). The metadata describes the layer as 'summertime, daytime LST' while calling it air temperature, and its ~18°C means look like 24-hour rather than daytime means, so the page says 'summer air temperature'. This is a difference from the London average, not the classic urban heat island differential against surrounding countryside, which this dataset does not give; London-wide heat-island maps on the Datastore use 2006 and 2011 data, older than the 10-year limit.
